Upon all this that righteous man, waxing bold and yielding to the exhortation of the mother of God, who is the handmaid of God in regard to the things which pertain to men, received into his aged arms Him who in infancy was yet the Ancient of days, and blessed God, and said, "Lord, now lettest Thou Thy servant depart in peace, according to Thy word: for mine eyes have seen Thy salvation, which Thou hast prepared before the face of all people; a light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of Thy people Israel." I have received from Thee a joy unmixed with pain. Do thou, O Lord, receive me rejoicing, and singing of Thy mercy and compassion. Thou hast given unto me this joy of heart. I render unto Thee with gladness my tribute of thanksgiving.
On the Gospel of Luke

And he blessed God and said: Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace. You see that not only the just of the New, but also of the Old Testament had the desire of future life in hope, to be released from the body, indeed they considered the way of peace to be laying down the earthly burden, as they did not doubt that they would have perpetual rest in the bosom of Abraham. Finally even Idithun, that is, the one who leaps over secular desires, after he had long silently contemplated many evils of the world, and had become fervent with internal meditation of the heart, finally spoke with his tongue, disclosing what he had done inwardly: Make known to me, O Lord, my end, and the number of my days, what it is, that I may know what is lacking in me. Behold, you have made my days old (Psalm 38). With these words, without a doubt, he reveals how greatly he hopes to attain solace in the end from the present calamities, which he desires to arrive as soon as possible.
On the Gospel of Luke

For my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples. Blessed are the eyes that see what Simeon saw: blessed are they who have not seen, and have believed (John 20). That very thing, he says, which you have prepared to be beheld with mind and faith by all nations, peoples, and tongues afterward, and which you foresaw was to be sought with hope and love, I now contemplate your salvation, long desired, with the eyes of both flesh and heart.
Against Marcion Book IV

The cleansing of the Syrian rather was significant throughout the nations of the world of their own cleansing in Christ their light, steeped as they were in the stains of the seven deadly sins: idolatry, blasphemy, murder, adultery, fornication, false-witness, and fraud.
Methodius Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna

And in addition to this, when besides the spectacle, and even beyond the spectacle, they heard an old man, very righteous, very worthy of credit, worthy also of emulation, inspired by the Holy Spirit, a teacher of the law, honoured with the priesthood, illustrious in the gift of prophecy, by the hope which he had conceived of Christ, extending the limits of life, and putting off the debt of death—when they saw him, I say, leaping for joy, speaking words of good omen, quite transformed with gladness of heart, entirely rapt in a divine and holy ecstasy; who from a man had been changed into an angel by a godly change, and, for the immensity of his joy, chanted his hymn of thanksgiving, and openly proclaimed the "Light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of Thy people Israel."
On the Gospel of Luke

A light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel. Light indeed for both the peoples, God's salvation, that is, Christ prepared by God the Father. Who is rather the glory of Israel, long hoped for by them, from whom pre-announced he has come, but he is said to be the revelation for the Gentiles, whose eyes of mind sunk in deep blindness and raised by no hope of the Lord's coming, he himself has deigned to visit, reveal, and illuminate alike. And it is well that the revelation of the Gentiles is preferred to the glory of Israel, because when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved. As the Psalmist also says: The Lord hath made known his salvation; he hath revealed his justice in the sight of the nations (Psalm 97); he joined on and says: He hath remembered his mercy to Jacob, and his truth to the house of Israel (Psalm 98).
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 16

"And", he says, "his father and mother were marveling over these things, which were said of him". Let us gather together into one the things that were said and written about Jesus at his birth, and then we shall be able to know that each single one is worthy of wonder. For which reason both the father was marveling — for so Joseph too was called, because he was a foster-father — the mother also was marveling over all the things "which were said of him". What then are the things that rumor had spread abroad concerning the little child Jesus? "There were shepherds in that region, keeping watch and observing the night-watches over their flock." At the very hour of Jesus' birth an angel came and said to them: "I announce to you great joy: go, and you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling-cloths and laid in a manger". The angel had not yet finished his words, and behold, "a multitude of the heavenly host" began to praise and bless God. When the shepherds, trembling, had beheld this, and "the angel had departed from them, they said to one another: Let us go to Bethlehem and see this deed which the Lord has shown us". They came and found the little child. Both they and the parents marveled over these things which had been done. And of Simeon it is written that he increased the report and was even a great part of the miracle. For he held the child in his arms and said: "Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace, according to your word, for my eyes have seen your salvation". The summit and, so to speak, the crown of the things that were noised abroad concerning Jesus, at which both his father and mother marveled, was the word of Simeon. For it did not suffice him to hold the little child and to speak out the things that were written concerning himself, but he "blessed" his father and his mother, and prophesied about the infant himself also, saying: "Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be contradicted. A sword shall pierce through your own soul also, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed".
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 17

Luke, who wrote: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore also that which will be born holy will be called the Son of God", and who plainly handed down to us that Jesus was the son of a virgin and was not conceived of human seed, this same Luke bore witness that Joseph was his father, saying: "And his father and mother were marveling at the things that were said of him". What reason, then, was there that he should record as father one who was not the father? He who is content with a simple exposition will say: the Holy Spirit honored him with the title of father, because he had nourished the Savior. But he who inquires into something more profound can say: since the order of generation is traced from David down to Joseph, lest Joseph seem to be named in vain — he who had not been the father of the Savior — in order that the order of generation might have its place, he was called the "father" of the Lord. "His father", then, "and mother were marveling at the things that were said of him" both by the angel and by the "multitude of the heavenly host", and also by the shepherds. For hearing all these things they marveled most vehemently.
On the Gospel of Luke

And his father and mother were marveling at what was said about him, and Simeon blessed them. He calls Joseph the father of the Savior, not that he was truly his father according to the Photinians, but since he was considered by all to be the father for the preservation of Mary's reputation. Nor did the Evangelist forget that he told she had conceived by the Holy Spirit and given birth as a virgin, but expressing the opinion of the people, which is the true law of history, he calls Joseph the father of Christ. Although in that way, he can rightly be called his father, as he is rightly understood as the husband of Mary without physical union, by the marriage bond itself, much more closely united indeed than if he had been adopted from elsewhere. For neither should Joseph be called the father of Christ because he had not begotten him through intercourse, since he would rightly be the father even if he had adopted someone not born from his wife elsewhere.
Against Marcion Book V

This stumbling-stone Marcion retains still. Now, what is that "foolishness of God which is wiser than men," but the cross and death of Christ? What is that "weakness of God which is stronger than men," but the nativity and incarnation of God? If, however, Christ was not born of the Virgin, was not constituted of human flesh, and thereby really suffered neither death nor the cross there was nothing in Him either of foolishness or weakness; nor is it any longer true, that "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; "nor, again, hath "God chosen the weak things of the world to confound the mighty; "nor "the base things" and the least things "in the world, and things which are despised, which are even as nothing" (that is, things which really are not), "to bring to nothing things which are" (that is, which really are).
On the Flesh of Christ

We acknowledge, however, that the prophetic declaration of Simeon is fulfilled, which he spoke over the recently-born Saviour: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign that shall be spoken against." The sign (here meant) is that of the birth of Christ, according to Isaiah: "Therefore the Lord Himself shall give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.
Exegetical Fragments

The Lord is represented to us as a horseman; and the "heel" points us to the "last times." And His "falling" denotes His death; as it is written in the Gospel: "Behold, this (child) is set for the fall and rising again of many." We take the "robber" to be the traitor. Nor was there any other traitor to the Lord save the (Jewish) people. "Shall rob him," i.e., shall plot against him. At the heels: that refers to the help of the Lord against those who lie in wait against Him. And again, the words "at the heels" denote that the Lord will take vengeance swiftly. He shall be well armed in the foot (heel), and shall overtake and rob the robber's troop.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 17

Then the Scripture says: "Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother: Behold, this one is set for the ruin and for the resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that shall be contradicted. And a sword shall pierce through your own soul, that the thoughts out of many hearts may be revealed". In what way the Savior came "for the ruin and for the resurrection of many" is to be contemplated. He who expounds simply can say that he came "for the ruin" of unbelievers and "for the resurrection" of believers. But he who is a careful interpreter says that by no means does one fall who has not first stood. Give me, then, who that one was who stood, and for whose "ruin" the Savior came, and also him who rises up. For surely he rises up who had before fallen. And so we must see whether perhaps the Savior did not come "for the ruin" of some and "for the resurrection" of others, but came for the same persons both "for ruin and for resurrection". "For judgment", he says, "I have come, that those who did not see may see, and those who saw may become blind". For there is in us one thing that saw before and afterward ceased to see, and another thing that did not see and afterward began to see. For example, I wish to see with those eyes with which I did not see before and which were afterward opened to me, since after the disobedience of both Adam and Eve "their eyes were opened", concerning which we treated in the previous discourse. But now we must interpret what this means which he says: "Behold, this one is set for the ruin and for the resurrection of many in Israel". It is fitting that I first fall, and, when I have fallen, that I afterward rise up well, lest the Savior be to me the cause of an evil ruin. But for this reason he made me fall, that I might rise up, and the ruin has been far more useful to me than that time in which I seemed to stand. For I was standing in sin at that time in which I was living in sin; and because I was standing in sin, the first benefit to me was that I should fall and die to sin. Finally, the holy prophets too, when they contemplated something more august, fell upon their faces; and they fell for this reason, that through this fall their sins might be more fully purged. This very thing the Savior first grants to you as well, that you may fall. You were a heathen — let the heathen fall in you; you loved harlots — let the fornicator first perish in you; you were a sinner — let the sinner fall in you, that you may thereafter rise again and say: "if we have died with him, we shall also live with him", and: "if we have been made conformable to his death, we shall be conformable also to his resurrection". This one, therefore, "is set for the ruin and for the resurrection of many in Israel", that is, among those who are able to behold with full keenness and reason, and "for a sign that shall be contradicted". Everything that the account relates concerning the Savior is contradicted. The mother is a virgin — it is a sign that is contradicted: the Marcionites contradict this sign and say that he was not at all born of a woman; the Ebionites contradict the sign, saying that he was born of man and woman just as we too are born. He had a human body, and this is a sign that is contradicted: for some say that he came from the heavens, others that he had a body such as ours, so that through the likeness of the body he might also redeem our bodies from sins and give us the hope of resurrection. He rose from the dead, and this is a sign that is contradicted: in what way he rose, whether he himself and such as he had died, or rather rose in a body of better substance; and there is endless dispute, some saying: he showed to Thomas the mark of the nails in his hands, others arguing from the opposite side: if he had the same body, how did he "enter through closed doors and stand"? You see, therefore, how by various arguments even the question of his resurrection is stirred up, and how it is "a sign that is contradicted". I think that this too, which was foretold by the mouth of the prophets, is a sign that is contradicted; for there are many heretics who assert that he was not at all foretold by the prophets. And what need is there for me to pursue many things? Everything that the account relates concerning him is a sign that is contradicted — not that those who believe in him contradict it (for we indeed know that all things which are written are true), but because among unbelievers everything that is written concerning him is a sign that is contradicted.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 16

What does this mean which he says: "behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel"? To this I have found something similar written in the Gospel according to John: "for judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may be made blind". Therefore, just as he came for judgment, that "those who do not see" of the nations "might see", and those who saw before, of Israel, "might be made blind", so he came "for the fall and rising of many". For at the coming of the Lord the Savior, those who had stood before fell down, and those who had fallen rose up. This is one interpretation of that which was said: "behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel". But there is also something deeper to be understood against those especially who bark against the Creator, and, gathering together from here and there out of the Old Testament testimonies which they do not understand, "deceive the hearts of the simple". For they say: behold, the God of the Law and the Prophets, see what sort he is. "I", he says, "will kill, and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal, and there is none who can deliver out of my hands". They hear: "I will kill", and they do not hear: "I will make alive"; they hear: "I will strike", and they disdain to hear: "and I will heal". On occasions of this kind they slander the Creator. Therefore, before I interpret what sense there is in: "I will kill and make alive, I will strike and heal", I will set against them a testimony of the Gospel and will say against the heretics — for there are countless heresies which receive the Gospel according to Luke —: If the Creator is bloodthirsty and only a judge and cruel because he says: "I will kill and make alive, I will strike and heal", it is most manifest that Jesus too is his son; for the same things are written of him: "behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel", not "for the rising" only, but also "for the fall". If it is evil to kill, let it be evil also to come "for the fall". What will they answer? Will they either withdraw from his worship, or will they seek some interpretation and flee to figurative readings, so that his coming "for the fall" may sound of kindness rather than of severity? And how will it be just, when something of this sort is found in the Gospel, to flee to allegories and new understandings, but when it is found in the Old Testament, at once to accuse and to accept no explanation, however probable it may be? But even this which follows: "for judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may be made blind", however much they seek to expound it, they will not be able to fulfill. But I, who desire to be of the Church and to be named and to bear a name not from any heresiarch, but from the appellation of Christ, and to have a name that is blessed upon the earth, and long to be and to be called a Christian both in work and in thought, seek an equal principle both in the old and in the new law. God speaks: "I will kill"; I am glad that God kills. For when the old man is in me and I still live as a man, I long that God may kill in me the old man and make me alive from the dead. For, he says, "the first man was of the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear also the image of the heavenly". According to this sense that also is understood: "for judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may be made blind". We all have in ourselves both sight and blindness. Adam both saw and did not see. Eve too, before her eyes were opened, is described as having seen: "the woman saw", it says, "the tree, that it was good for eating and most delightful to the eyes for seeing: and taking of the fruit of the tree she ate, and gave to her husband, and they ate". Therefore they were not blind, but saw. Then it follows: "and their eyes were opened". Therefore they had been blind and did not see, whose eyes were afterward opened; but those who had seen well before, after they transgressed the commandment of the Lord, began to see badly, and afterward, as the offense crept in, they lost the sight of obedience. Thus I understand also that which God says: "Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I, the Lord God?" There is an eye of the body, with which we behold these earthly things, an eye according to the sense of the flesh, of which the Scripture says: "walking vainly, puffed up by the sense of the flesh". To this we have another, contrary and better, that savors of divine things; and because it was blind in us, Jesus came to make it see, that those who did not see might see, and those who saw might be made blind. According to this sense, then, is that also to be understood which we now have in hand: "behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel". I have something in me that stands badly and raises itself up in the pride of sin: let this fall, let this be pulled down; and if it falls, that which had before fallen down will, rising, stand. My "inner man" once lay struck down, and the outer stood erect. Before I believed in Jesus, the good in me lay down, the evil stood. After he came, then what was evil in me fell down, and that was fulfilled: "always carrying about the dying of Jesus in the body", and that: "put to death your members upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, luxury, idolatry, sorceries", and the rest. The fall of all these has been made useful. And of this fall it is said: "Wherever the corpse shall be, there the eagles will be gathered". For a corpse (cadaver) has received its name from falling (a casu). Good is this fall, to which Jesus first comes, and he cannot bring about the rising unless the fall has gone before. Let him come first to destroy what was evil in me, so that, when that is destroyed and put to death, there may rise up in me and be made alive that which is good, so that in it may follow the kingdom of heaven: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 105: ON THE DARKENING OF THE SUN

HOW THE PROPHECY AGREES WITH THE GOSPEL, CONCERNING THE DARKENING OF THE SUN AND CERTAIN OTHER THINGS. — Since at the Lord’s first coming it was foretold that the sun would be darkened at his passion, at the very hour when it is proved to have happened, that is, at midday, for therefore it is written in the prophet Amos: “And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord, I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day” (Amos 8:9). On that day, therefore, from the sixth hour the sun was darkened until the ninth hour, and therefore the prophecy of the aforementioned prophet was fulfilled. The image of this event, which is to occur at the Lord’s second coming, was shown in the Lord’s passion; for at the end, when the Lord begins to come to judge the world, the heavenly lights will be released from their service, as the Lord says: “In those days the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light” (Matt. 24:29). Joel the prophet has not omitted this either, so that, being signified by many, it may without doubt be believed to be fulfilled. For therefore he said: “The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and revealing day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2:31). As far as appears, this more fittingly belongs to the second coming; for then it will be openly revealed to all, as Scripture says: “Then every eye shall see him, and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him, and those who crucified him” (Rev. 1:7). Therefore, if in both comings it is contained that the sun shall be darkened in those days, what is that day on which Scripture rings that the sun and moon shall be increased? For among other things Isaiah says: “And there shall be upon every high mountain, and upon every high hill, streams running with water in that day, when many shall perish and when the towers shall fall. And the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, in the day when the Lord shall heal the brokenness of his people” (Isa. 30:25–26), and so forth. What day can be understood, on which the Lord promised to heal the brokenness of his people? I think this is the day which Zacharias, the father of John, pointed out when he said: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and performed the redemption of his people. And he has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been since the world began, that he would deliver us from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us, to perform mercy with our fathers” (Luke 1:68–72). And Simeon, among other things, said: “This child is set for the fall and for the rise of many in Israel” (Luke 2:34). This fall is that of the scribes and Pharisees and the rulers of the Jews, whom the prophet signified by the towers. These, therefore, falling through unbelief, others rose up by believing, who had previously seemed weak and sick through negligence. Where the Savior says: “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (Jn. 9:39); so that those who by the practice and knowledge of the Law seem to be lights may be blinded through unbelief, but the blind, that is, the unlearned or publicans, may see by believing. Their weaknesses the prophet foretold that the Savior would bear (Isa. 53:11). And so at this time of the Savior it came to pass, as we read in the Gospel, that “he took our infirmities and bore our diseases” (Matt. 8:17). All these things indeed were completed and fulfilled in the Savior’s passion: for therefore the salvation of the human race, both in heaven above and in the lower regions, was both redeemed and confirmed, since the prophecy of the aforementioned Zacharias encompasses both. For here above they were freed from the crushing of enemies by the intervention of mercy; and there below, in the underworld, when they were snatched from Tartarus. For all who hoped in the promised Christ were awaiting his coming, that, death having been conquered, they might be freed from Hades. Therefore he said: “To perform mercy with our fathers.” If anyone, however, understands this salvation also to be contained in the second coming, yet in both comings, especially in the second, the sun will be turned into darkness and the moon will not give her brightness: how then shall we perceive the sun and moon to be increased on the day when the Lord will visit his people, when in both times, in which the liberation of the people was begun and completed, we read that the sun and moon are not diminished but darkened? Unless, clearly, we understand the sun and moon to be compared to the saints; just as in another place we read that the saints are made equal to the heavenly lights, with the Apostle Paul preaching that among these men the saints in this world appear as luminaries. And in the Gospel: “Then the righteous shall shine like the sun” (Matt. 13:43). For the Lord calls righteous works “light”: therefore he says, “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). Those, therefore, who, having left all that is theirs, follow the Lord for the sake of righteousness and holiness, are compared to the sun and moon as being honored sevenfold; as the Lord says: “There is no one who leaves house, or wife, or children, or fields, who will not receive seven times as much in this age” (see Luke 18:29–30). Those, then, who are now honored sevenfold can be understood to be believed in the future to become seven degrees brighter than the rest; so that their resurrection is compared to the sun and moon, while that of the others is like the stars. Therefore the brightness of the saints, which is honored sevenfold here, obtains another sevenfold in the resurrection, so that one who here has the brightness of the moon will receive the brightness of the sun in the future; and one who here is compared to the sun will be believed then to receive seven times as much. Therefore the prophet Isaiah foretold that by comparison with the sun and moon the merits of the saints would be increased, and not without reason. For if the Lord himself is called the Sun of righteousness, and the saints will be like him, as the Apostle John says: “When he appears, we shall be like him” (1 Jn. 3:2), then fittingly the saints are signified in the sun, yet the aforementioned prophet shows the sun to be greater than the moon by seven degrees For when it shows that the moon, like the light of the sun, will exist in the future, but the sun will be seven times as great; it certainly means, in the manner of speaking, that the moon will be increased sevenfold more than the sun, so that the moon will then be such as the sun is now: although the reasoning here concerns the saints, under this explanation of the luminaries it has nevertheless partly revealed their measure, so that after the increase of the sun and the moon, a saint will again be as much greater as the sun once was; and as much as one saint now differs from another saint, so much will one differ from another in the future after the reward.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 73: ON SIMEON'S PROPHECY TO MARY

WHAT IS IT THAT SIMEON SAYS TO MARY, THE MOTHER OF THE LORD, AMONG OTHER THINGS: “THIS CHILD IS SET FOR THE FALL AND THE RISING OF MANY IN ISRAEL; AND A SWORD, HE SAYS, SHALL PIERCE THROUGH YOUR OWN SOUL ALSO, THAT THE THOUGHTS OF MANY HEARTS MAY BE REVEALED” (Luke 2:34–35)? — Simeon, a holy man, commended by divine oracles, spoke through the Holy Spirit about what would happen to people because of Christ, namely, that He would be a cause of ruin to those who, while they seemed to themselves to stand through their observance and skill in the Law, would nevertheless fall through distrust of Christ’s works, being severed from the promise given to the Fathers; but for those who possessed almost no dignity in the Law, yet believed in Christ, He would be a resurrection in Israel. [So that those who were formerly unworthy and useless might become worthy of God, and those who thought themselves to be something might be rejected.] This is what the Lord says in another place: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (Jn. 9:39). Indeed, it was not the doctors of the Law, nor the Pharisees, nor the scribes who followed Christ, but fishermen, uneducated and country men. Therefore the Lord says: “Father, I thank you because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25). But when he adds, saying, “And a sword shall pierce through your own soul also, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed,” he certainly meant that even Mary, through whom the mystery of the Incarnation of the Savior was accomplished, would waver at the death of the Lord; yet in such a way that she would be strengthened by the honor of the resurrection and by the power of the Lord. For all, in a certain stupor, doubted at the death of the Lord. Yet they did not remain in doubt. For the sword therefore passes through the soul, if doubt does not remain in the mind, but is driven out when the former strength returns and renews itself. [For who would not hesitate when he saw Him who called Himself the Son of God so humbled that He descended even to death? And because, as I have said, all uncertainty was to depart at the resurrection of the Lord, he said that the sword would pass through, not that it would fall upon, or touch some passing limb. Just as a sword that is hurled and passes close by a man causes fear and yet does not strike him, so doubt would cause grief, yet would not kill: because it did not settle in the soul, but passed through, as if touching the hearts of the disciples only as a shadow. Indeed, Cleopas and the other disciple, as they went to Emmaus, sad along the road, said among other things to the Lord Himself, not knowing that He was the Lord, “We were hoping that it was He who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). They doubted, but, as soon as they recognized the Lord, the doubt passed away.] So it is also said of Joseph, that “iron passed through his soul” (Ps. 105:18). For he, though innocent, was long held in prison; it is no wonder if he doubted somewhat regarding God’s judgment about him; but because he hoped more in God, he did not remain in uncertainty. For a person is judged in that point to which he is most inclined. The Apocalypse of John confirms this. For it says: “The fearful and unbelieving shall have their part in the lake which burns with fire and sulphur” (Rev. 21:8). Therefore, the one who does not remain in doubt is snatched from death: this is to escape death; for to doubt about God or about Christ is death. And therefore, the one who ceases to doubt escapes death.

And he said to Mary his mother: Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be spoken against. Blessed indeed in the rising for he is the light, the glory of the people of Israel, as he said: I am the resurrection and the life: he who believes in me, though he were dead, shall live, and whoever lives and believes in me shall never die (John XI). But how is he set for the fall, except that he is also a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense? That is to say, a downfall to those who stumble upon the word and do not believe. Of whom he himself says: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not be guilty of sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin (John XXII). He is set not only in himself, but also in his preachers for the fall and rising of many, as the Apostle testifies who says: For we are to God the aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing. To the one, we are an aroma that brings death; to the other, an aroma that brings life (II Cor. II). For whoever hears the word preached by the Apostle and follows it in love rises with a good aroma and is saved. Whoever follows it in hatred falls and perishes by the same aroma. But the sign that will be spoken against, understand as the faith in the Lord's cross. Of which the Apostle Paul says Jews: For as concerning this sect, it is known to us that it is spoken against everywhere (Acts XXVIII). And the Apostle himself: For we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Greeks foolishness (I Cor. I).
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 17

Then Simeon says: "and a sword shall pierce through your own soul". What is this sword, which pierced not only through the hearts of others, but even through the heart of Mary? It is plainly written that in the time of the passion all the apostles were scandalized, the Lord himself also saying: "you shall all be scandalized in me this night". Therefore they were all scandalized to such a degree that even Peter, the chief of the apostles, denied him three times. What are we to think — that, while the apostles were scandalized, the mother of the Lord was immune from scandal? If she suffered no scandal at the passion of the Lord, then Jesus did not die for her sins. But if "all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified by his grace and redeemed", then surely Mary too was scandalized at that time. And this is what Simeon now prophesies, saying: "and your own soul" — you who know that you gave birth as a virgin without a man, you who heard from Gabriel: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you" — "the sword" of unbelief "shall pierce through", and you will be struck by the blade of doubt, and your thoughts will tear you in different directions, when you see him, whom you had heard to be the Son of God and knew to have been begotten without the seed of a man, crucified and dying and subjected to human torments and at the last tearfully complaining and saying: "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me". "And" therefore "a sword shall pierce through your soul, that the thoughts out of many hearts may be revealed". There were evil thoughts in men, which were for this reason revealed, that, being brought out into the open, they might be destroyed and slain, and cease to be, being dead, and that he who died for us might slay them. For as long as the thoughts were hidden and not brought out into the open, it was impossible for them to be utterly slain. Hence we too, if we have sinned, ought to say: "I have made my sin known to you, and my iniquity I have not hidden. I said: I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord". For if we do this and reveal our sins not only to God but also to those who are able to heal our wounds and sins, our sins will be blotted out by him who says: "behold, I will blot out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist".

Neither letter nor history teaches that Mary passed from this life by the bodily suffering of death; for it was not the soul, but the body, that was pierced by the material sword. And therefore, the prudence of Mary shows her to be not unaware of the heavenly mystery. For the living word of God, and sharp and piercing with every sharpest sword, penetrates even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and searches the thoughts and secret intentions of the heart; for all things are naked and open to the Son of God, to whom the secrets of consciences do not deceive.
On the Gospel of Luke

And a sword shall pierce through your own soul also. No history teaches that blessed Mary departed from this life by the sword's killing, especially since it is not the soul, but the body that is usually killed by iron. Hence it must be understood that this sword, of which it is said: And a sword is in their lips (Psalm LVIII), passed through her soul, meaning the sorrow of the Lord's passion. Even though she knew Christ to be the Son of God and thus would not doubt he would overcome death, she, however, could not without sorrow witness her flesh and blood being crucified. For the iron that is said to have transpierced Joseph's soul is best understood as severe mental tribulation.

That the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed. It was uncertain once who among the Jews would accept the grace of Christ, which they surely knew was to come, and who would rather reject it. But upon hearing of His birth, with the thoughts of hearts soon revealed, King Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. The shepherds, with fear and joy, resounded praises to God, announced the message of peace to men. With His teaching and power being spread abroad, some flocked to Him as a teacher of truth, others fled from Him as a deceiver. With His sign of the cross raised, some mocked blasphemously as if justly condemned to death, others mourned bitterly as if the author of life were dying. And even to this day, and to the end of the present age, the sword of most severe tribulation does not cease to pierce through the soul of the Church, while it considers many hearing the Word of God and rising with Christ, but many more falling away from belief. With the thoughts of many hearts revealed, where the best seed of the Gospel is sown, there the weeds of vices either prevail more than they should or, gravely to say, alone germinate and reign.

We produce, too, our remaining (evidences). For we now hasten to modern proofs. On the threshold of the Gospel, Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, "who both recognised the infant Lord, and preached many things about Him to such as were expecting the redemption of Israel," after the pre-eminent distinction of long-continued and single-husbanded widowhood, is additionally graced with the testimony of "fastings" also; pointing out, as she does, what the duties are which should characterize attendants of the Church, and (pointing out, too, the fact) that Christ is understood by none more than by the once married and often fasting.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 17

After the prophecy of Simeon, because it was necessary that women too should be saved, there came a prophetess, a woman, of whom it is written: "and there was Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser". How beautiful the order! The woman does not come before the man, but first comes Simeon, who took up the infant and held him in his arms, then the woman, whose words indeed are not set down, but it is said generally that "she confessed to the Lord and spoke of him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Jerusalem". And rightly did the holy woman deserve to receive the spirit of prophecy, because by long chastity and long fastings she had ascended to this height. See, women, the testimony of Anna, and imitate it! If it should ever happen to you that you lose your husbands, consider what is written of her: "she lived seven years from her virginity with a husband" and the rest; for this reason she was a "prophetess"; for the Holy Spirit did not dwell in her at random and by chance. It is good and best, if any woman is able to possess the grace of virginity; but if she has not been able to do this, and it has befallen her to lose her husband, let her remain a widow. And this she ought to have in mind not only after the death of her husband, but even while he lives, so that, even if her own will and resolve do not come to pass, she may be crowned by the Lord and may say: this I vow and promise, that if anything human, which I do not wish for, should befall me, I will do nothing else than remain undefiled and a widow. But now second and third and fourth marriages — to say nothing of more — are found in the Church, and we are not unaware that such a union will cast us out of the kingdom of God. For just as not only fornication but also second marriages exclude a man from ecclesiastical dignities — for neither a bishop nor a presbyter nor a deacon nor a widow can be twice-married — so perhaps the twice-married man will also be cast out from the assembly of the "firstborn and undefiled", the "Church, which has no spot or wrinkle"; not that he is sent into the eternal fire, but that he has no part in the kingdom of God. I recall that, when I was interpreting that which is written to the Corinthians: "to the church of God which is at Corinth, with all who call upon him", I said that there is a distinction between the "church" and those "who call upon" the name of the Lord. For I think that the man of one marriage and the virgin and he who perseveres in chastity belong to the church of God, but that he who is twice-married, although he may have had a good manner of life and abound in the other virtues, nevertheless does not belong to the "church" and to that number which "has no wrinkle or spot, or any such thing", but belongs to a second rank and to those "who call upon" the name of the Lord, and who are indeed saved in the name of Jesus Christ, yet are by no means crowned by him: to whom be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

Therefore Simeon prophetized, the Virgin had prophesied, the one united in marriage had prophesied, and so too should the widow; so that neither the profession nor the sex may be lacking. And for this reason Anna is introduced with both the wages of widowhood and the character of such; so that she may be truly believed to have been worthy to announce the redeemer of all. Since we have described her merits elsewhere, when we exhorted widows, in this place as we hasten to other matters, we do not think it necessary to repeat. However, she spent eighty-four years of widowhood not idly; because both seven decades and two forties seem to represent a sacred number.
On the Gospel of Luke

And there was Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, from the tribe of Asher; she had advanced in many days, etc. According to the history of her devout conversation and equally venerable age, and worthy in all aspects to bear witness to the incarnate Lord, Anna is taught to have been. According to the mystical understanding, because she signifies the Church, which in the present is as if widowed by the death of her spouse and Lord, the number of her years of widowhood also designates the time of the Church, when established in the body, she journeys as a pilgrim away from the Lord, and with the affection of great devotion, keeping the thresholds of the heavenly temple, awaits that daily coming of the Lord. Concerning this He says: We shall come and make our abode with him (John 14). For seven times twelve make eighty-four. And indeed seven refers to the course of this world, which revolves in seven days. Twelve, on the other hand, pertains to the perfection of apostolic doctrine. Therefore, whether it is the universal Church, or any faithful soul who cares to dedicate the entire span of their life to apostolic institutions, it is praised as if multiplying seven by twelve, and serving the Lord in the figurative eighty-four years. Also as the time of seven years, during which she stayed with her husband, most fittingly corresponds to the time of the Lord's incarnation. For by the number seven (as I said), the perfection of time is usually indicated. But there, due to the privilege of the Lord's majesty by which He taught in the flesh, the simple number of seven years is expressed. Here, on account of the apostolic summit of dignity, seven years are multiplied by twelve. However, it pleases the mysteries of the Church that Anna is interpreted as grace and that she is the daughter of Phanuel, which means face of God, singing with the Psalmist: The light of your face, O Lord, is signed upon us (Psalm 4). And she descends from the tribe of Asher, which means blessed, which among the twelve patriarchs is the eighth in the order of birth. About which number, because it is sacred to the New Testament, it has been repeatedly emphasized.

Let not us, then, who are in Christ-that is, always in the lights cease from praying even during night. Thus the widow Anna, without intermission praying and watching, persevered in deserving well of God, as it is written in the I Gospel: "She departed not," it says, "from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day." Let the Gentiles look to this, who! are not yet enlightened, or the Jews who have remained in darkness by having forsaken the light. Let us, beloved brethren, who are always in the light of the Lord, who remember and hold fast what by grace received we have begun to be, reckon night for day; let us believe that we always walk in the light, and let us not be hindered by the darkness which we have escaped. Let there be no failure of prayers in the hours of night-no idle and reckless waste of the occasions of prayer. New-created and newborn of the Spirit by the mercy of God, let us imitate what we shall one day be. Since in the kingdom we shall possess day alone, without intervention of night, let us so watch in the night as if in the daylight. Since we are to pray and give thanks to God for ever, let us not cease in this life also to pray and give thanks.

When, then, to these sacred rites, prophecy and the priesthood had been jointly called, and that pair of just ones elected of God—Simeon, I mean, and Anna, bearing in themselves most evidently the images of both peoples—had taken their station by the side of that glorious and virginal throne,—for by the old man was represented the people of Israel, and the law now waxing old; whilst the widow represents the Church of the Gentiles, which had been up to this point a widow,—the old man, indeed, as personating the law, seeks dismissal; but the widow, as personating the Church, brought her joyous confession of faith and spake of Him to all that looked for redemption in Jerusalem, even as the things that were spoken of both have been appositely and excellently recorded, and quite in harmony with the sacred festival. And when they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their city Nazareth. In this place, Luke omitted what he knew to be sufficiently explained by Matthew, namely that the Lord, after these things, so that he would not be found and killed by Herod, was taken by his parents to Egypt, and after Herod's death, he thus returned to Galilee, and began to inhabit his city Nazareth. For the evangelists individually are accustomed to omit certain things that they either saw were mentioned by others, or foresaw would be mentioned by others in the spirit, so that in the continuous series of their own narrative, they appear to have omitted nothing. My Lord Jesus was born, and his parents went up to Jerusalem to fulfill the things that had been commanded in the law, and to offer for him "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons". Simeon held him in his arms, as was read a little while ago, and prophesied concerning him the things that the account relates. And after everything was completed according to custom, the parents returned. In what year was Jesus at that time? He was assuredly still a little child, and yet he "grew and became strong and was filled with wisdom" and grace; he had not yet completed the forty days of purification, he had not yet come to Nazareth, and already he was receiving all wisdom. Scripture could have said: "he grew and became strong, and received the Spirit"; but because "he had emptied himself, taking the form of a servant", as soon as the sacrifice was offered for his purification, that which he had emptied out he filled up again — not that his body was thereupon made greater, but that something more sacred might be shown, as Scripture reports: "but the child grew and became strong and was filled with wisdom". Let us inquire whether anywhere else it is written of a little child: "he grew and became strong", so that by comparing many passages we may be able to understand what more is said in the case of our Lord. We read concerning John: "but the child grew and became strong", and yet there is not added: "and was filled with wisdom", but rather: "he became strong in spirit". But here, concerning the Lord, it says: "he grew and became strong and was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him". All these things were said of a child who had not yet completed twelve years.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 19

Since some who seem to believe the holy Scriptures deny the divinity of the Savior, as though for the glory of the almighty God, it seems just to me that they should be taught from the authority of those very Scriptures that something divine came into a human body, and not only into a human body, but also into a human soul. Yet, if we attend carefully to the meaning of the Scriptures, that soul had something more than the rest of human souls. For every human soul, before it comes to virtue, is defiled by vices. But the soul of Jesus was never stained with the filth of sin. Indeed, before he reached the twelfth year of his age, the Holy Spirit writes concerning him in the Gospel of Luke: "But the boy grew and was strengthened and was filled with wisdom". This human nature does not admit, that one should be filled with wisdom before twelve years. It is one thing to have a part of wisdom, another to be filled with wisdom. Let us not doubt, therefore, that something divine appeared in the flesh of Jesus, and something beyond not only man, but beyond every rational creature as well. And "he grew", it says. For "he had humbled himself, taking the form of a servant", and by the same power by which "he had humbled himself", he grows. He had appeared weak, because he had taken up a weak body, and for that reason he is again strengthened. The Son of God "had emptied himself", and therefore he is again filled with wisdom. "And the grace of God was upon him". Not when he came to adolescence, not when he was teaching openly, but while he was still a little child, he had the grace of God; and just as all things in him had been marvelous, so also his childhood was marvelous, that the wisdom of God might be fulfilled.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke, Sermon V

TO say that the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, being filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon Him, must be taken as referring to His human nature. And examine, I pray you, closely the profoundness of the dispensation: the Word endures to be born in human fashion, although in His divine nature He has no beginning nor is subject to time: He Who as God is all perfect, submits to bodily growth: the Incorporeal has limbs that advance to the ripeness of manhood: He is filled with wisdom Who is Himself all wisdom. And what say we to this? Behold by these things Him Who was in the form of the Father made like unto us: the Rich in poverty: the High in humiliation: Him said to "receive," Whose is the fulness as God. So thoroughly did God the Word empty Himself! For what things are written of Him as a man show the manner of the emptying. For it were a thing impossible for the Word begotten of God the Father to admit ought like this into His own nature: but when He became flesh, even a man like unto us, then He is born according to the flesh of a woman, and is said also to have been subject to the things that belong to man's state: and though the Word as being God could have made His flesh spring forth at once from the womb unto the measure of the perfect man, yet this would have been of the nature of a portent: and therefore He gave the habits and laws of human nature power even over His own flesh.
Be not therefore offended, considering perchance within thyself, How can God increase? or how can He Who gives grace to angels and to men receive fresh wisdom? Rather reflect upon the great skill wherewith we are initiated into His mystery. For the wise Evangelist did not introduce the Word in His abstract and incorporeal nature, and so say of Him that He increased in stature and wisdom and grace, but after having shown that He was born in the flesh of a woman, and took our likeness, he then assigns to Him these human attributes, and calls Him a child, and says that He waxed in stature, as His body grow little by little, in obedience to corporeal laws. And so He is said also to have increased in wisdom, not as receiving fresh supplies of wisdom,----for God is perceived by the understanding to be entirely perfect in all things, and altogether incapable of being destitute of any attribute suitable to the Godhead:----but because God the Word gradually manifested His wisdom proportionably to the age which the body had attained.
The body then advances in stature, and the soul in wisdom: for the divine nature is capable of increase in neither one nor the other; seeing that the Word of God is all perfect. And with good reason he connected the increase of wisdom with the growth of the bodily stature, because the divine nature revealed its own wisdom in proportion to the measure of the bodily growth.
On the Gospel of Luke

And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him. The distinction of the words is notable, because the Lord Jesus Christ, in that he was a child, that is, had assumed the condition of human frailty, had to grow and become strong. But in that he was also the Word of God and the eternal God, he did not need to become strong nor did he need to grow. Hence, he is very rightly said to be full of wisdom and grace. Wisdom because in him dwells all the fullness of deity bodily. Grace because to the same mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ, great grace was given, so that from the moment he began to be man, he might be perfect and God. Similar to this is what John writes, that he is full of grace and truth, he himself setting forth that same excellence of divinity of truth, which Luke commends under the name of wisdom.

"And so his parents went according to custom to Jerusalem to the solemn day of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old". Observe carefully, that before he was twelve years old, he was being filled with the wisdom of God and with the other things that are written of him.
On the Gospel of Luke

And his parents went every year to Jerusalem, at the feast of Passover. You see this evangelist, among the four creatures, not without reason compared to the calf, which, as if designated for sacrifices, revolves around the temple and Jerusalem with the course of his narrative. For indeed at the beginning he places a priest praying at the altar, establishes a multitude of people in the courts of the temple, soon sends Mary, having conceived the Lord, to Jerusalem, introduces her into the house of the High Priest. There he recounts the birth of the Baptist, and immediately after the birth, transfers the Lord with an offering. He leads him there every year with his parents, and at the age of twelve inserts him into the choir of doctors in the temple. Where among other things, he says astonishing things to the wise: Because it behooves me to be in the things of my Father (Luke 2). And after such things, he concludes his Gospel with the disciples praising God in the temple.
Homilies on the Gospels 1.19

The Lord's coming every year to Jerusalem for the Passover with his parents is an indication of his human humility. It is characteristic of human beings to gather to offer God the votive offerings of spiritual sacrifices, and by plentiful prayers and tears to dispose their Maker toward them. Therefore the Lord, born a human being among human beings, did what God, by divine inspiration through his angels, prescribed for human beings to do. He himself kept the law which he gave in order to show us, who are human beings pure and simple, that whatever God orders is to be observed in everything. Let us follow the path of his human way of life. If we take delight in looking upon the glory of his divinity, if we want to dwell in his eternal home in heaven all the days of our lives, it delights us to see the Lord's will and to be shielded by his holy temple. And lest we be forever buffeted by the wind of wickedness, let us remember to frequent the house, the church of the present time, with the requisite offerings of pure petitions.

After the Evangelist had said, that Jesus advanced in wisdom and grace with God and men, he next shows that what he says is true: for he carries Him to Jerusalem in company with the holy Virgin, upon the summons of the feast: and then he says that He remained behind, and was afterwards found in the temple sitting in the midst of the doctors both asking and answering questions regarding those things, as we may feel sure, which were spoken of old by the law: and that He was wondered at by all for His questions and answers. On the Gospel of Luke

And when he was twelve years old, as they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day, and having completed the days as they returned, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem. The one who, from birth, indeed from human conception, was approved by clear signs of miracles showing that he is God, even then, as soon as the time of age was appropriate, began reverently to reveal and open both his natures, namely, what in truth of divine majesty belonged to the Father, and what, according to the frailty of human assumption, belonged to the mother. Nor without foresight did he reveal the first rudiments of his faith at twelve years old, which by the ministry of the twelve apostles was to be revealed and elucidated throughout the world. We can also say this, that as with the number seven, similarly the number twelve, which consists of the multiplied parts of seven, may designate the totality and perfection of things or times. And for this reason, that it is fitting for all places or times to be occupied, the light rightly takes its beginning from the number twelve. Therefore, it is not idly said that he appeared to have been unmindful of his parents, but that he instructs us, because not only before his own parents, but even before Abraham was made, he is, he delights rather to reside in the city and temple of God, as if by paternal right.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18
But when he was twelve years old, he remained behind in Jerusalem. His parents, not knowing this, seek him anxiously and do not find him.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 19

When therefore, as we have said, he was twelve years old, and the days of the solemnity had been completed according to custom, and his parents were returning, "the boy remained in Jerusalem and his parents did not know it". And here understand something more sublime than human nature undergoes. For he did not simply "remain" while his parents were ignorant of where he was; but just as it is written in the Gospel of John, when the Jews were lying in wait for him and he slipped away out of their midst and did not appear, so also now I think that the boy remained in Jerusalem and that his parents were ignorant of where he had remained. Nor let us wonder that they are called parents, of whom the one merited the name because of the childbirth, the other because of his service to the mother and the father.
On the Gospel of Luke

And his parents did not know. But assuming that he was in the company, they went a day's journey, and sought him among relatives and acquaintances, and not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem searching for him. Someone might ask how the Son of God, reared with such care by his parents, could have been forgotten and left behind as they went away. To this, it must be answered that it was the custom of the sons of Israel that during festive times, whether they converged on Jerusalem or returned to their own places, the men and women would walk separately in choruses, and infants or children could go with either parent indifferently. And thus, the blessed Mary or Joseph might have thought by turns that the boy Jesus, whom they did not see accompanying themselves, had returned with the other parent.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 19

And when they sought him, they did not find him "among their kinsfolk". For human kinship could not contain the Son of God. They did not find him "among their acquaintances", because the divine power was greater than mortal acquaintance and knowledge.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18

They seek "among their kinsfolk", they seek "in the company", they seek "among their acquaintances", and in all these they do not find him. Jesus, then, is sought by his parents, by the father who had been his nurse and companion when he went down to Egypt, and yet he is not found immediately when he is sought. For Jesus is not found among relatives and kinsmen of the flesh, not among those who are joined to him bodily. In the company of many my Jesus cannot be found.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18

Learn where those seeking him find him, so that you too, seeking with Joseph and Mary, may find him. And seeking him, it says, "they found him in the temple". Not anywhere in some other place, but "in the temple", and not simply "in the temple", but "in the midst of the teachers, hearing them and questioning them". You too, therefore, seek Jesus "in the temple" of God, seek him in the Church, seek him among the masters who are "in the temple" and do not go out from it; for if you seek in this way, you will find him. Moreover, if anyone says that he is a master and does not have Jesus, that man is a master in name only, and therefore Jesus, the word of God and wisdom, cannot be found with him. He was found, it says, "in the midst of the teachers". Just as it is written in another place concerning the prophets, so also now understand "in the midst of the teachers". "If", it says, "anything is revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first keep silence". They find him "sitting in the midst of the teachers", and not only "sitting", but also "questioning and hearing them". And now too Jesus is present; he questions us and hears us speaking.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 19

Where, then, do they find him? "In the temple"; for there the Son of God is found. If ever you too shall seek the Son of God, seek first the temple, hasten thither, there you will find Christ, the Word and the wisdom, that is, the Son of God. But because he was a little one, he is found "in the midst of the teachers", sanctifying and instructing them. Because he was a little one, he is found "in the midst" not teaching them, but "questioning", and this in accordance with the duty of his age, that he might teach us what befits children, however wise and learned they be, namely that they should rather hear their masters than desire to teach, and should not vaunt themselves with vain display. He was questioning, I say, the masters, not that he might learn something, but that in questioning he might instruct. For from one fountain of teaching flows both to question and to answer wisely; and it belongs to the same knowledge to know what you should ask and what you should answer. It was fitting that the Savior should first become a master of learned questioning, that afterward he might respond to questions according to the reason and word of God: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 2.63

Nor is it unimportant that, mindful of his earthly parents, who were certainly filled with the wisdom and grace of God according to the flesh, he is found in the temple after three days; so that he might provide evidence that after three days of his triumphant passion on the heavenly throne, and with divine honor, he would offer himself as resurrected for our faith, who was believed to be dead.
On the Gospel of Luke

And it happened after three days, they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, listening to them and asking questions. As a fountain of wisdom sits in the midst of the doctors, but as an example of humility, he first seeks to listen and ask questions of the doctors rather than to teach the unlearned. So that the little ones may not be ashamed to learn from their elders, and he himself, for the sake of human age appropriateness, is not ashamed to listen to men, though he is God. So that the weak may not dare to teach, he, as a boy, wished to be taught by asking questions, who by the power of divinity provided the word of knowledge to his very doctors.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18

"And all", it says, "were amazed". At what were they "amazed"? Not at his questions, although these too were marvelous, but "at his answers". For it is one thing to ask, another to answer. He was questioning the teachers, and because at times they could not answer, he himself answered them concerning the things about which he had asked. But that an answer signifies not the alternation of conversing but teaching in the holy scriptures, let the divine law teach you. "Moses spoke, and God answered him by a voice". That answer was concerning the matters about which the Lord was instructing the ignorant Moses. Sometimes Jesus asks, sometimes he answers, and as we said above, although his questioning is marvelous, nevertheless his answering is far more marvelous.
On the Gospel of Luke

And all who heard him were astonished at his wisdom and answers, and seeing him, they were amazed. Note the distinction of words, and diligently examine the mysteries of your salvation and faith. They were astonished at what they heard from him, and seeing him, they were amazed. And they were all the more astonished at the wisdom of his answers, the more they despised the fewness of his years seeing it. His tongue revealed divine wisdom, but his age pretended human infirmity. Truly, let these things astound the doctors of the Jews as if they were new, and let them be disturbed by a doubtful amazement among the high things they hear and the weak things they see. But let us, knowing that this is he of whom the Prophet once rejoiced, saying, "A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God" (Isaiah 9); let us in no way wonder at him, who has been made a little child and yet has always remained what he was, namely, God and mighty, displaying at times signs of his divinity, at times signs of his humanity to those he wished to instruct. But let us give thanks to him with faith, hope, and charity, because he who was great and exceedingly praiseworthy, though we did not know him, was born as a little child for us, so that by growing and advancing among the little ones, he might gradually lead them to embrace the secrets of his virtue and greatness.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18

Therefore, that we too may hear him and that he may set before us questions which he himself may resolve, let us beseech him and seek him with the utmost labor and sorrow, and then we shall be able to find him whom we seek. For it is not written in vain: "I and your father have been seeking you with sorrow". He who seeks Jesus must seek not negligently, not carelessly, not in passing, as some seek and therefore cannot find him. But let us say: "with sorrow we seek you".
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 19

There follows: "sorrowing we were seeking you". I do not think that they sorrowed for this reason, because they supposed the boy had strayed or perished; nor could it happen that Mary, who knew that she had conceived of the Holy Spirit, who had heard both the angel speaking and the shepherds hastening and Simeon prophesying, should fear that she might lose the boy through his wandering off. Remove this opinion especially from Joseph, to whom it had been commanded by the angel that he should take the boy and go to Egypt, who had heard: "do not fear to take Mary your wife; for that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit". It could never come to pass that he should dread as lost the infant whom he had known to be divine. The sorrow and the seeking of the parents sounds like something other than the simple reader understands. Just as you, if ever you read the Scriptures, seek in them the meaning with a certain sorrow and torment—not that you should judge the Scriptures to have erred or to contain something amiss, but because they hold within a word and reason of truth, and you are unable to find what is true: so also they were seeking Jesus, lest perhaps he had withdrawn from them, lest, leaving them, he had migrated to other things and—what I think more likely—lest he had returned to the heavens, intending, when it should please him, to descend again. "Sorrowing", therefore, they were seeking the Son of God.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke, Sermon V

His mother certainly knew that He was not the child of Joseph, but she so speaks to avoid the suspicions of the Jews. And upon her saying, that "Thy father and I have sought Thee sorrowing," the Saviour answers...
On the Gospel of Luke

And his mother said to him: Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I, sorrowing, have been seeking you. And he said to them: Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be about my Father's business? Not Joseph, who provided nothing for his generation except service and affection, whence he is called father both by the evangelist and by Mary herself for his faithful service; Christ does not deny him as his parent, but simply and openly indicates who is his true Father, equally to us and to them. He does not reproach them for seeking him as a son, but rather compels them to raise the eyes of their mind to what is owed to him who is the eternal Son. For as he is both God and man, he now exhibits the heights of divinity, now the depths of human frailty. As a man, he questions the elders, as God he responds to matters which astonish the elders and the learned. As the Son of God, he dwells in the temple of God, and as the son of man, he returns with his parents where they command.
Against Heresies (Book I, Chapter 20)

Some passages, also, which occur in the Gospels, receive from them a colouring of the same kind, such as the answer which He gave His mother when He was twelve years of age: "Wist ye not that I must be about My Father's business?" Thus, they say, He announced to them the Father of whom they were ignorant.
Against Praxeas

This He Himself, in those other Gospels also, testifies Himself to have been from His very boyhood: "Wist ye not," says He, "that I must be about my Father's business? " Satan likewise knew Him to be this in his temptations: "Since Thou art the Son of God.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 20

Mary and Joseph were seeking Jesus "among their kinsfolk" and did not find him; they were seeking him "in the company" and could not find him. They sought him "in the temple", and not simply "in the temple", but with the teachers, and "in the midst of the instructors" they find him. Wherever the teachers may be, there "in the midst of the teachers" Jesus is found, if only the teacher sits "in the temple" and never departs from it. Jesus profited his own teachers, and those whom he seemed to be questioning he taught, speaking "in their midst", and in a certain way he stirred them up to seek out the things they did not know, and to investigate the things which, up to that point, they were unable to know—whether they knew them or were ignorant of them. Jesus, then, is found "in the midst of the teachers", and once found he says to those who sought him: "Why is it that you were seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?" First, understanding this simply, let us arm ourselves against the impious heretics who say that the Creator is not the Father of Christ Jesus, nor the God of the Law and the prophets. Behold, the Father of Christ is asserted to be the God of the temple. Let the Valentinians blush when they hear Jesus saying: "I must be in my Father's house". Let all the heretics blush who receive the Gospel according to Luke and yet despise the things that are written in it. Let these things, as I said, be understood in the simpler sense. But since it is added: "they, however, did not understand the saying", let us more diligently sift out the meaning of the Scripture.

Were they so foolish and senseless that they did not know what he was saying—whether this, which he says, "I must be in my Father's house", signified "in the temple", or whether it signifies something else more profound, and something that edifies the hearers more? Each one of us, if he is good and perfect, is a possession of God the Father. Generally, therefore, concerning all, the Savior taught that he ought not to be anywhere except among those who are the Father's. If any one of you belongs to God the Father, he has Jesus in his midst. Let us indeed believe the one who says: "I must be in my Father's house". And I suspect that this is the more rational and living and true temple of God, rather than that one which was built typologically by an earthly work. Hence, as he was in that temple typologically, so also typologically he withdrew from it. For he "went out of the temple" that was earthly, saying: "Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate", and leaving that house he came to the possession of God the Father—the churches scattered throughout the whole world—and says: "I must be in my Father's house". Then, therefore, "they did not understand the word which he spoke to them".
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18

And when we have said this, he will answer our laboring soul that seeks him with sorrow, and will say: "Do you not know that I must be in my Father's house?". Where are the heretics, where are the impious and the mad, who assert that the law and the prophets do not belong to the Father of Jesus Christ? Surely Jesus was "in the temple" that was built by Solomon, and he confesses that that temple belongs to his Father, whom he revealed to us, whose Son he said he was. Let them answer, how one God is good and another just. Since, therefore, the Savior is the Son of the Creator, let us together praise the Father and the Son, whose is the law, whose also is the temple: to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke, Sermon V

Here then first He makes more open mention of Him Who is truly His Father, and lays bare His own divinity: for when the holy Virgin said, Child, why hast Thou so done unto us? then at once shewing Himself to transcend the measure of human things, and teaching her that she had been made the handmaid of the dispensation in giving birth to the flesh, but that He by nature and in truth was God, and the Son of the Father That is in heaven, He says, Did ye not know that I must be at My Father's? Here let the Valentinians, when they hear that the temple was God's, and that Christ was now at His own, Who long before also was so described in the law, and represented as in shadows and types, feel shame in affirming, that neither the Maker of the world, nor the God of the law, nor the God of the temple, was the Father of Christ.
Homilies on the Gospels 1.19

Clearly the abode in the hearts of the elect of the holy Trinity, the nature of whose divinity is one and indivisible, cannot be disparate. Therefore, when he was sitting in the temple, the Lord said, "I must be about my Father's business," and this is a declaration of his power and glory which are co-eternal with God the Father's. However, when he returned to Nazareth, he was subject to his parents, and this is an indication of his true humanity as well as an example of humility. He was subject to human beings in that human nature in which he is less than the Father. Hence he himself said, "I go to the Father because the Father is greater than I." In that human nature, he was made a little less than the angels. In that other nature, however, in which he and the Father are one, and in virtue of which he does not go to the Father only now and then but is always in him, all things were made through him, and he is before all things.
On the Gospel of Luke

And they did not understand the word that he spoke to them. And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them. How much an example of piety and humility in the Lord! His parents did not understand the word that he spoke to them about his divinity, and yet he, not ungrateful for their human diligence towards him, descended to where they commanded, and was subject to them. For what would the teacher of virtue be if he did not fulfill the duty of piety? What else among us than that he would do what he wanted us to do? He deferred to a man, he deferred to a maidservant. For she herself says: Behold the handmaid of the Lord (Luke 1). He deferred to the simulated father, he deferred to the true father who is God. And indeed he had preserved his mother, born of a virgin, as a virgin and chaste; indeed, he did not differ from the father by will, by act, or by time. In order that, being admonished by his example, we might recognize what we owe to our parents, who suffer so much for us. The Arians are wont to say that the Son was imperfect because he said, The Father is greater than I (John 14). But what marvel if from human reception he asserts himself lesser than the Father in heaven, from which he was also subject to his parents on earth?
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 20

And at the same time attend to this: that, as long as he was in the possession of his Father, he was above. And because Joseph and Mary did not yet have full faith, for that reason they could not remain above with him, but he is said to have come down with them. Frequently Jesus comes down with his disciples, nor is he always dwelling on the mountain, nor without end does he hold to sublime things. On the mountain he is with Peter, with James, with John, and again in another place with the rest of the disciples. Further, because those who labored under various sicknesses were not able to ascend the mountain, therefore he "came down and came" to those who were below. Now also it is written: "he came down with them and came to Nazareth and was subject to them". Let us learn, children, to be subject to our parents: the greater is subject to the lesser.
